screens.title: Host Provisioning with Red Hat Satellite
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how Red Hat Satellite centralizes host provisioning so you can deploy consistent RHEL systems at scale. We will follow the key provisioning methods Satellite supports — PXE network boot, discovery for unknown bare metal, image-based provisioning for clouds, and tight compute resource integration with platforms like vCenter or OpenStack. You will also learn how Host Groups and provisioning templates turn manual installs into repeatable artifacts, and how Kickstart files with embedded ERB provide dynamic configuration at install time. As an example, we'll customize a Kickstart template to install and enable a web server automatically during the post-install phase. Understanding these pieces is essential because automated provisioning reduces human error, speeds environments creation in DevOps pipelines, and ensures compliance via consistent Content Views and partition tables. A common pitfall is assuming a compute platform alone completes provisioning; in practice you must configure networking services like DHCP and TFTP and validate template parameters. By the end you will know which Satellite components to configure, how a provisioned VM moves from A P I call to registered host, and how to avoid frequent failures such as missing TFTP or package content. Keep an eye on the Kickstart and PXE templates: they are the automation heart of provisioning.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Host Provisioning Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Host Provisioning with Red Hat Satellite

Automate installs, register systems, and scale deployments using PXE, discovery, image-based methods, and compute integrations.

Duration: 15–25 min demo
Why this matters

Provisioning with Satellite removes manual installation steps, enforces content control, and integrates VM lifecycle with configuration management so environments are reproducible and auditable.

PXE & Kickstart: Network boot plus automated install.
Host Groups: standardize settings for many hosts.
Coming up
  • Configure compute resources and Host Groups.
  • Customize Kickstart templates with ERB for dynamic installs.
  • Troubleshoot common PXE and content issues.
Explore Key Topics
PXE Provisioning
Network boot, TFTP, and Kickstart deliver unattended installs to bare-metal or VMs.
Kickstart Templates
ERB-driven Kickstart files let you inject host parameters and run post-install scripts like enabling httpd.
Host Groups
Group defaults for OS, partitioning, content view and provisioning templates for repeatable builds.
Visual Concept
Provisioning Path
Compute API → VM creation → PXE network boot → Kickstart → Post-install registration
Automation Heart
Provisioning templates + Host Groups + Content Views = repeatable, validated installs
Quick takeaway

Satellite ties compute, network boot, and templating into a single provisioning workflow so hosts come online ready and registered.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the provisioning methods Satellite supports, configure the server and compute resources for PXE-based installs, author and customize Kickstart templates with ERB, and provision a host from Satellite to completion. You will practice creating a Host Group that bundles Content Views, partition tables, and provisioning templates so a single selection produces consistent VMs. We also cover the necessary networking pieces — DHCP, TFTP, and HTTP — and how they interact with PXE. A concrete outcome is a Kickstart template that installs and starts an httpd service during the post-install phase, which you will see in the activity. Finally, you will learn common failure modes and remedies, such as validating TFTP accessibility, checking package availability in the Content View, and verifying compute credentials. These objectives matter because managing many hosts manually is error-prone; mastering Satellite provisioning lets you scale, enforce compliance, and reduce time to deployment. After this chapter you should be able to design Host Groups and templates that make provisioning predictable and auditable.

Applied Objectives

Concrete tasks you will configure and test in the hands-on activity.

Practical tasks

Activity Preview

Misconception

Creating a VM in a compute resource does not guarantee successful install; network boot and provisioning templates must be correct.

Pro tip

screens.title: What is Satellite Integrated Provisioning?
screens.narratorSegment: Integrated provisioning in Red Hat Satellite is the coordinated process that creates a host — whether bare metal or virtual — and performs the initial operating system installation and registration using Satellite-managed artifacts. In plain terms, Satellite becomes the single control plane for creating VMs on a compute platform or booting bare-metal via PXE, supplying a Kickstart, applying configuration via Host Groups, and registering subscriptions during post-install. The benefit is consistent systems from first boot: partitioning, package selection, networking, and post-install scripts are defined centrally and versioned with Content Views and Host Groups. A concrete example is provisioning a RHEL 8 web server: you create a Host Group named "RHEL8 Web Servers" that references a Kickstart template containing the %packages and %post sections to install and enable httpd. When Satellite provisions the VM, the Kickstart runs automatically and the service is active at first boot. A common misconception is to think Satellite only manages subscriptions; in fact, its provisioning automation is equally important and requires correct network services, templates, and compute credentials. As a takeaway, mastering integrated provisioning means you can define the desired host state before the machine exists and have Satellite realize that state reliably.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › What is Integrated Provisioning?
Definition and benefits

Integrated provisioning centralizes host creation, OS installation, and registration so every host follows organizational standards automatically.

Consistency
Templates and Host Groups ensure identical partitioning, packages, and post-install tasks.
Speed
Automated installs reduce time to deploy new nodes in DevOps workflows.
Auditability
Content Views and Host Groups produce repeatable, reviewable artifacts for compliance.
Example
Host Group: RHEL8 Web Servers
Contains RHEL 8 OS, partition table, Kickstart template that adds httpd in %packages and enables it in %post.
Common misconception
Satellite provisioning is more than subscription registration; it requires network services and templates to be correct for the install to complete.
Provisioning flow (conceptual)
  1. Add compute resource and Host Group.
  2. Create host entry; Satellite creates VM and configures DHCP/TFTP.
  3. VM PXE boots, downloads kernel/initramfs, and fetches Kickstart.
  4. Kickstart performs install and runs %post to configure services and register the host.
Key Takeaway

Provisioning automates the full lifecycle from VM creation to registration using templated artifacts.

Check your understanding

If a VM is created but does not complete install, what networking or template items should you validate first?

screens.title: Provisioning Methods: PXE, Discovery, Image, Compute
screens.narratorSegment: Satellite supports several provisioning approaches, and choosing the right one depends on hardware state and environment. PXE-based provisioning is the common choice for bare-metal and many virtual machines because it boots the target over the network, fetches kernel and initramfs via TFTP, and then retrieves a Kickstart to perform an automated install. Use PXE when you control the network and can provide DHCP and TFTP. Discovery-based provisioning is for unknown bare-metal that you cannot pre-configure; hosts boot a discovery image that reports hardware details to Satellite so you can create an inventory entry and provision without prior setup. Image-based provisioning is ideal for cloud or virtualization platforms where you can provision from prepared images; this saves time for identical appliances but requires image management. Compute resource integration is not a separate install method but a capability that lets Satellite create and manage VMs through APIs like vCenter, Red Hat Virtualization, or OpenStack. A concrete example: in a lab where you control networking and want full partition control, PXE plus Kickstart gives granular control; in a public cloud, provisioning from images is faster. A common misconception is thinking image-based always removes the need for templates; you still need provisioning templates or post-boot configuration for registration and final state. Consider network access, hardware discovery needs, and the level of configuration control when selecting the method.

keyIdea.text: Select PXE for fine-grained installs, discovery for unknown bare metal, image-based for cloud speed, and always integrate compute APIs for VM lifecycle.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Provisioning Methods
Methods compared
PXE-based Provisioning
Network boot that downloads kernel/initramfs via TFTP and pulls a Kickstart to perform automated install.
Use when: controlled network
Discovery-based Provisioning
Boot an unknown host into a discovery image to inventory hardware and then provision without prior config.
Use when: unknown bare metal
Image-based Provisioning
Deploy from pre-built images in cloud or virtual environments for fast clones.
Use when: cloud images available
Compute Resource Integration
Satellite creates and manages VMs via APIs to platforms such as vCenter, OpenStack or KVM.
Use when: automate VM lifecycle
Example scenario

If you run a private cloud, use compute integration with image-based provisioning for fast fleet builds. If you provision racks of servers, use PXE to customize disks and packages at install time.

Practical considerations
  • PXE requires DHCP and TFTP accessibility and may need Capsule configuration.
  • Discovery helps when hardware inventory is unknown but requires a discovery image boot path.
  • Image-based provisioning reduces install time but needs image maintenance for updates.
  • Compute credentials must be valid; otherwise Satellite can’t create or power VMs.
Common mistake

Assuming image-based provisioning removes the need to register and configure the host; you still need post-boot steps or templates for registration and final configuration.

screens.title: PXE Provisioning Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: PXE provisioning follows a series of network and automation steps that must all succeed for an automated install to complete. First, the target machine requests an IP address via DHCP. The DHCP response must include the correct TFTP server and boot filename so the client can download kernel and initramfs. If DHCP or TFTP are misconfigured, the client will not fetch boot files and the install fails immediately. Next, after the client boots the kernel and initramfs, it will contact Satellite or the configured HTTP server to fetch a Kickstart file. Satellite generates a host-specific Kickstart using ERB templates and host parameters; this Kickstart contains all installer directives such as partitioning, package choices, and %post scripts. During %post, you can run scripts to install packages, enable services, and register the system with Satellite using subscription-manager. Finally, once installation finishes, the host should contact Satellite, appear in the host list, and be manageable. A concrete example: a VM boots, DHCP points it to the Capsule's TFTP, the kernel loads, the Kickstart injects a command to install and enable httpd, and the host registers. A common misconception is blaming the compute resource when PXE fails; often the issue is TFTP or DHCP misconfiguration or a firewall blocking TFTP/HTTP.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › PXE Provisioning Walkthrough
Step-by-step PXE flow
  1. DHCP provides IP and TFTP server/boot filename; ensure DHCP entries point to your Capsule or Satellite TFTP.
  2. TFTP serves kernel and initramfs; a blocked port or wrong path stops the boot.
  3. Kickstart retrieval via HTTP: Satellite generates a host-specific Kickstart template using ERB variables.
  4. Installation proceeds according to Kickstart: partition table, package selection, network config, and %post scripts.
  5. Post-install registration uses subscription-manager to register the host with Satellite and attach entitlements.
Supporting checks
  • Confirm TFTP access from the target network and that firewall rules allow UDP 69.
  • Validate the Kickstart template syntax before provisioning.
  • Ensure packages referenced are available in the assigned Content View.
  • Verify compute credentials can create and power the VM.
Example
A VM boots, gets DHCP with TFTP equal to the Capsule, downloads kernel, then obtains Kickstart which instructs the installer to add httpd and enable it in %post. After reboot, subscription-manager registers the host.
Key Takeaway

PXE provisioning requires a chain of working services; validate each link when debugging failures.

Common mistake

Assuming the compute platform is at fault when the client fails to download kernel/initramfs; often DHCP/TFTP or firewall issues are the cause.

Check your understanding

If a client boots but cannot fetch Kickstart, which services and logs should you inspect first?

screens.title: Compute Resources and Host Groups
screens.narratorSegment: Compute resources let Satellite interact with virtualization platforms or cloud endpoints to create, start, and stop virtual machines. You register vCenter, OpenStack, Red Hat Virtualization, or KVM hypervisors as compute resources. The practical implication is that Satellite can perform VM lifecycle actions and attach provisioning templates automatically. Host Groups then build on top of compute resources: a Host Group is a bundle of defaults — Content View, Lifecycle Environment, Operating System, Architecture, Partition Table, Provisioning Template, and Compute Profile. By selecting a Host Group when creating a host, most fields are pre-populated and consistent. For example, to provision a fleet of RHEL 8 web servers you create a Host Group referencing "Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8", the "Kickstart RHEL8 Web Server" template, the "Kickstart Default" partition table, and a compute profile pointing to your vCenter compute resource. This means a single form submission creates a VM with the correct disk layout, packages, and compute parameters. A common misconception is thinking Host Groups manage runtime configuration beyond initial provisioning; they set installation-time defaults, while post-install configuration and ongoing management require configuration management or Ansible roles. As a takeaway, combine compute resources and Host Groups to reduce manual setup steps and scale consistent VM creation across your platform.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Compute Resources & Host Groups
Compute Resources

Register your virtualization endpoints so Satellite can talk to vCenter, OpenStack, RHV, or KVM and automate VM creation and power actions.

What to validate
  • API endpoint and credentials are correct and have permissions to create VMs.
  • Compute profiles map to templates, networks, and datastore choices.
  • Satellite can power on and off VMs via the compute API.
Host Groups
Host Groups are the standardization layer that pre-fills provisioning fields for repeatable deployments.
Host Group example
RHEL8 Web Servers
Content View: Base RHEL 8 & Custom Apps / Development. OS: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8. Partition Table: Kickstart Default. Provisioning Template: Kickstart RHEL8 Web Server. Compute Profile: vCenter-Standard.
Key Takeaway

Use Host Groups to enforce installation defaults and compute profiles to target the correct environment.

Misconception

Host Groups set install-time defaults; they do not replace configuration management for ongoing system drift control.

screens.title: Operating Systems, Partition Tables, and Templates
screens.narratorSegment: Satellite's provisioning requires explicit Operating System entries that represent the RHEL variants you will install. These entries capture architecture, default partition tables, and which provisioning templates apply. Partition tables are reusable definitions of disk layouts and are applied during Kickstart-driven installs, determining where root, swap, and other file systems are created. Provisioning templates — PXELinux/Grub2 for boot and Kickstart templates for the installer — are the mechanism that connects the boot process to the install directives. Think of the modeling as a hierarchy: Operating System entries reference partition tables and provisioning templates; Host Groups pick an Operating System which then applies those artifacts to generated Kickstarts. For a concrete example, define an Operating System for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, attach a "Kickstart Default" partition table, and associate the Kickstart default provisioning template. That template can embed variables with ERB to reflect host-specific values when Satellite generates the Kickstart. A common error is editing a Kickstart template without validating its ERB; syntax problems cause Kickstart generation to fail. As a takeaway, maintain a clear mapping of OS entries → partition tables → templates so your Host Groups reliably produce correct Kickstarts and disk layouts.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › OS, Partition & Templates
Hierarchy of provisioning artifacts
Operating System entries in Satellite define the family of the OS and link to partition tables and provisioning templates. Partition tables define disk layouts. Provisioning templates provide the PXE boot and Kickstart content used at install time.
Partition Tables
Reusable disk layout definitions applied by the installer during Kickstart processing.
Provisioning Templates
PXELinux/Grub2 templates for boot and Kickstart templates with ERB for dynamic values.
Key Takeaway

Keep a clear mapping of Operating System entries to partition tables and templates to ensure Kickstarts are generated with correct layout.

Concrete example
OS: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8
Architecture: x86_64. Partition Table: Kickstart Default. Provisioning Template: Kickstart default or custom Kickstart RHEL8 Web Server.
Pitfall

Editing a template without validating ERB syntax or the variables referenced can cause Kickstart generation to fail for hosts using that OS entry.

Check

Before scaling, test a Host Group with the OS entry and template to verify partitioning and package installation succeed.

screens.title: Kickstart Templates and ERB Customization
screens.narratorSegment: Kickstart templates are standard Anaconda files augmented with ERB so Satellite can inject host-specific variables at generation time. The typical pattern is to place static Kickstart directives and use ERB tags to substitute passwords, network settings, or activation keys. For example, setting the root password dynamically uses an ERB variable that Satellite replaces when creating the host-specific Kickstart. You can also include a %post section to run post-install commands such as installing packages, enabling services, and creating files. A concrete example from this chapter shows a %post that installs httpd, enables and starts the service, and creates a simple index. html so the server is ready after the first boot. Always be mindful that Kickstart templates must not leak sensitive information in plaintext; avoid embedding secrets directly and use host parameters or secure mechanisms. A common error is a small syntax mistake in ERB or Kickstart directives that breaks generation or causes the installer to abort. As a practical step, clone and validate the default template, add the %packages and %post snippets, test on a single Host Group, and inspect the generated Kickstart and VM console to confirm the expected actions ran.

A concrete example from this chapter shows a %post that installs httpd, enables and starts the service, and creates a simple index. html so the server is ready after the first boot. Always be mindful that Kickstart templates must not leak sensitive information in plaintext; avoid embedding secrets directly and use host parameters or secure mechanisms. A common error is a small syntax mistake in ERB or Kickstart directives that breaks generation or causes the installer to abort. keyIdea.title: ERB makes Kickstarts dynamic
keyIdea.text: Use ERB variables to inject host parameters and %post scripts to perform post-install configuration like installing and enabling httpd.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Kickstart & ERB walkthrough
Kickstart snippet (ERB example)
# Root password
rootpw --iscrypted <%= root_pass %>

%post --log=/var/log/anaconda/post-install.log

# Install additional packages
dnf install -y httpd mariadb-server

# Enable and start services
systemctl enable --now httpd
systemctl enable --now mariadb

echo "Post-installation script completed."

%end
This template uses an ERB variable root_pass supplied by host parameters or Host Group defaults. The %post block installs and enables services, creating a ready host on first boot.
Pro tip

Keep logs in %post to aid troubleshooting and avoid storing plain-text secrets inside templates.

Testing and validation
Clone the Kickstart default template, edit, and preview the generated Kickstart for a sample host. Validate ERB syntax and ensure variables referenced are defined in the Host Group or host parameters.
Example activity

Add httpd to %packages and include a %post creating /var/www/html/index.html with a short message. Attach the template to a Host Group and provision one host to verify the service is running post-install.

Common mistake

A single missing ERB tag or Kickstart directive typo can prevent Kickstart generation or cause install failure; always preview and test on one VM first.

screens.title: Provisioning a Host: Step-by-step in Satellite
screens.narratorSegment: Provisioning a host in Satellite is a reproducible sequence of steps. Start by ensuring compute resources are registered under Infrastructure → Compute Resources and their credentials validate. Next, create or edit a Host Group with the desired Content View, Lifecycle Environment, Operating System, Partition Table, and Provisioning Template. When creating a new host, select the Host Group which pre-fills most fields; supply a unique FQDN and IP, and choose the compute resource and compute profile for VM sizing. After submitting, Satellite will request the compute A P I to create the VM, add DHCP and TFTP entries, and generate a host-specific Kickstart. The VM is powered on, PXE boots, downloads boot files, and the Kickstart runs. Following the completion of installation and %post tasks, the system registers via subscription-manager and appears in Satellite’s host inventory. A practical example is creating a host from the "RHEL8 Web Servers" Host Group so that httpd is installed automatically. A typical misconception is expecting the compute A P I operation to be instantaneous; in many environments there is a creation delay and you should monitor both Satellite and compute logs. As a final takeaway, validate each step — compute registration, Host Group configuration, template selection, and generated Kickstart — to ensure a successful end-to-end provisioning.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Provisioning a Host
Checklist
  1. Validate compute resource credentials and API reachability.
  2. Create Host Group with OS, partition table, provisioning template, and compute profile.
  3. Create Host: name, IP, select Host Group and compute resource.
  4. Submit and monitor VM creation, PXE boot, and Kickstart execution.
  5. Confirm post-install registration and services are active.
Example: RHEL8 Web Server

Create a Host Group "RHEL8 Web Servers" that points to the Kickstart template adding httpd. Create a host that uses the Host Group; Satellite creates the VM, runs the Kickstart, and after install you can browse the custom index.html.

Monitoring and logs

Check the VM console to see kernel and initramfs load, review the generated Kickstart in Satellite, and if issues occur, consult the Satellite logs and the compute platform's task logs to find creation or credential failures.

Key Takeaway

Provisioning is a linear sequence; monitor each stage and confirm generated artifacts are correct before scaling.

Misconception

Assuming VM creation implies successful install. Creation is separate from PXE boot and Kickstart execution which must be verified.

Try this

Before mass provisioning, test one Host Group-host combination and confirm the expected services and registration occur.

screens.title: Common Provisioning Failures and Remedies
screens.narratorSegment: When provisioning fails, a focused troubleshooting approach speeds resolution. Start by determining where the failure occurred: before kernel load (DHCP/TFTP), during installation (Kickstart syntax or missing packages), or during post-install (registration or service start). If the VM cannot download kernel or initramfs, verify DHCP options and TFTP accessibility and that firewall rules permit UDP 69. If Kickstart is missing or syntactically invalid, preview the generated Kickstart in Satellite and validate ERB variables are defined in the Host Group or host parameters. If package installation fails, check that the requested packages are present in the assigned Content View and that repositories are synchronized. For compute issues where Satellite cannot create VMs, verify compute resource credentials and A P I permissions. DNS problems can prevent hosts from contacting Satellite for registration; check forward and reverse DNS and ensure hostnames resolve. A concrete remediation example: a PXE client fails to find the Kickstart because the TFTP path is misconfigured; updating DHCP to provide the correct TFTP server or fixing Capsule TFTP settings resolves the issue. A common misconception is over-indexing on a single log; effective troubleshooting uses both the VM console and Satellite logs to triangulate the root cause. As a takeaway, isolate the stage of failure, verify service reachability, and confirm template and content availability.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Troubleshooting Provisioning
Network boot failure

Symptoms: client never downloads kernel. Checks: DHCP options, TFTP server address, firewall UDP 69, Capsule TFTP settings.

Kickstart or ERB errors

Symptoms: Kickstart missing or installer aborts. Checks: preview generated Kickstart, validate ERB variables exist, test syntax.

Missing packages

Symptoms: dnf errors during install. Checks: ensure packages are in the assigned Content View and repositories synchronized.

Compute credential issues

Symptoms: Satellite cannot create or power a VM. Checks: API endpoint reachability, correct credentials and permissions.

DNS and registration

Symptoms: host does not appear in Satellite inventory after install. Checks: forward/reverse DNS, network access to Satellite, subscription-manager registration logs.

Remediation example

If TFTP is misaddressed in DHCP, update the DHCP server or Capsule settings to point clients to the correct TFTP server, then retry the PXE boot.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how Red Hat Satellite centralizes host provisioning so you can deploy consistent RHEL systems at scale. We will follow the key provisioning methods Satellite supports — PXE network boot, discovery for unknown bare metal, image-based provisioning for clouds, and tight compute resource integration with platforms like vCenter or OpenStack. You will also learn how Host Groups and provisioning templates turn manual installs into repeatable artifacts, and how Kickstart files with embedded ERB provide dynamic configuration at install time. As an example, we'll customize a Kickstart template to install and enable a web server automatically during the post-install phase. Understanding these pieces is essential because automated provisioning reduces human error, speeds environments creation in DevOps pipelines, and ensures compliance via consistent Content Views and partition tables. A common pitfall is assuming a compute platform alone completes provisioning; in practice you must configure networking services like DHCP and TFTP and validate template parameters. By the end you will know which Satellite components to configure, how a provisioned VM moves from A P I call to registered host, and how to avoid frequent failures such as missing TFTP or package content. Keep an eye on the Kickstart and PXE templates: they are the automation heart of provisioning.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the provisioning methods Satellite supports, configure the server and compute resources for PXE-based installs, author and customize Kickstart templates with ERB, and provision a host from Satellite to completion. You will practice creating a Host Group that bundles Content Views, partition tables, and provisioning templates so a single selection produces consistent VMs. We also cover the necessary networking pieces — DHCP, TFTP, and HTTP — and how they interact with PXE. A concrete outcome is a Kickstart template that installs and starts an httpd service during the post-install phase, which you will see in the activity. Finally, you will learn common failure modes and remedies, such as validating TFTP accessibility, checking package availability in the Content View, and verifying compute credentials. These objectives matter because managing many hosts manually is error-prone; mastering Satellite provisioning lets you scale, enforce compliance, and reduce time to deployment. After this chapter you should be able to design Host Groups and templates that make provisioning predictable and auditable.

This second objectives screen focuses on applied tasks you will practice. First, you will add and validate a compute resource so Satellite can create and control VMs through vCenter, KVM, or OpenStack APIs, and understand credential pitfalls that prevent VM creation. Second, you will build and associate a Host Group that contains the operating system selection, partition table, provisioning template, and compute profile so a single choice produces a full VM configuration. Third, you will edit a Kickstart template to include a %packages and a %post section that installs and enables httpd, creates an index page, and logs actions for troubleshooting. Finally, you will run a test provision and learn to read Satellite logs and the VM console to confirm the kernel, initramfs, and Kickstart were fetched correctly. These tasks matter because hands-on configuration reveals where network or content mismatches break automation, and the example web server shows how a practical service can be baked into the first boot. Practicing these outcomes builds confidence that provisioning will succeed in production.

Integrated provisioning in Red Hat Satellite is the coordinated process that creates a host — whether bare metal or virtual — and performs the initial operating system installation and registration using Satellite-managed artifacts. In plain terms, Satellite becomes the single control plane for creating VMs on a compute platform or booting bare-metal via PXE, supplying a Kickstart, applying configuration via Host Groups, and registering subscriptions during post-install. The benefit is consistent systems from first boot: partitioning, package selection, networking, and post-install scripts are defined centrally and versioned with Content Views and Host Groups. A concrete example is provisioning a RHEL 8 web server: you create a Host Group named "RHEL8 Web Servers" that references a Kickstart template containing the %packages and %post sections to install and enable httpd. When Satellite provisions the VM, the Kickstart runs automatically and the service is active at first boot. A common misconception is to think Satellite only manages subscriptions; in fact, its provisioning automation is equally important and requires correct network services, templates, and compute credentials. As a takeaway, mastering integrated provisioning means you can define the desired host state before the machine exists and have Satellite realize that state reliably.

Satellite supports several provisioning approaches, and choosing the right one depends on hardware state and environment. PXE-based provisioning is the common choice for bare-metal and many virtual machines because it boots the target over the network, fetches kernel and initramfs via TFTP, and then retrieves a Kickstart to perform an automated install. Use PXE when you control the network and can provide DHCP and TFTP. Discovery-based provisioning is for unknown bare-metal that you cannot pre-configure; hosts boot a discovery image that reports hardware details to Satellite so you can create an inventory entry and provision without prior setup. Image-based provisioning is ideal for cloud or virtualization platforms where you can provision from prepared images; this saves time for identical appliances but requires image management. Compute resource integration is not a separate install method but a capability that lets Satellite create and manage VMs through APIs like vCenter, Red Hat Virtualization, or OpenStack. A concrete example: in a lab where you control networking and want full partition control, PXE plus Kickstart gives granular control; in a public cloud, provisioning from images is faster. A common misconception is thinking image-based always removes the need for templates; you still need provisioning templates or post-boot configuration for registration and final state. Consider network access, hardware discovery needs, and the level of configuration control when selecting the method.

PXE provisioning follows a series of network and automation steps that must all succeed for an automated install to complete. First, the target machine requests an IP address via DHCP. The DHCP response must include the correct TFTP server and boot filename so the client can download kernel and initramfs. If DHCP or TFTP are misconfigured, the client will not fetch boot files and the install fails immediately. Next, after the client boots the kernel and initramfs, it will contact Satellite or the configured HTTP server to fetch a Kickstart file. Satellite generates a host-specific Kickstart using ERB templates and host parameters; this Kickstart contains all installer directives such as partitioning, package choices, and %post scripts. During %post, you can run scripts to install packages, enable services, and register the system with Satellite using subscription-manager. Finally, once installation finishes, the host should contact Satellite, appear in the host list, and be manageable. A concrete example: a VM boots, DHCP points it to the Capsule's TFTP, the kernel loads, the Kickstart injects a command to install and enable httpd, and the host registers. A common misconception is blaming the compute resource when PXE fails; often the issue is TFTP or DHCP misconfiguration or a firewall blocking TFTP/HTTP.

Compute resources let Satellite interact with virtualization platforms or cloud endpoints to create, start, and stop virtual machines. You register vCenter, OpenStack, Red Hat Virtualization, or KVM hypervisors as compute resources. The practical implication is that Satellite can perform VM lifecycle actions and attach provisioning templates automatically. Host Groups then build on top of compute resources: a Host Group is a bundle of defaults — Content View, Lifecycle Environment, Operating System, Architecture, Partition Table, Provisioning Template, and Compute Profile. By selecting a Host Group when creating a host, most fields are pre-populated and consistent. For example, to provision a fleet of RHEL 8 web servers you create a Host Group referencing "Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8", the "Kickstart RHEL8 Web Server" template, the "Kickstart Default" partition table, and a compute profile pointing to your vCenter compute resource. This means a single form submission creates a VM with the correct disk layout, packages, and compute parameters. A common misconception is thinking Host Groups manage runtime configuration beyond initial provisioning; they set installation-time defaults, while post-install configuration and ongoing management require configuration management or Ansible roles. As a takeaway, combine compute resources and Host Groups to reduce manual setup steps and scale consistent VM creation across your platform.

Satellite's provisioning requires explicit Operating System entries that represent the RHEL variants you will install. These entries capture architecture, default partition tables, and which provisioning templates apply. Partition tables are reusable definitions of disk layouts and are applied during Kickstart-driven installs, determining where root, swap, and other file systems are created. Provisioning templates — PXELinux/Grub2 for boot and Kickstart templates for the installer — are the mechanism that connects the boot process to the install directives. Think of the modeling as a hierarchy: Operating System entries reference partition tables and provisioning templates; Host Groups pick an Operating System which then applies those artifacts to generated Kickstarts. For a concrete example, define an Operating System for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, attach a "Kickstart Default" partition table, and associate the Kickstart default provisioning template. That template can embed variables with ERB to reflect host-specific values when Satellite generates the Kickstart. A common error is editing a Kickstart template without validating its ERB; syntax problems cause Kickstart generation to fail. As a takeaway, maintain a clear mapping of OS entries → partition tables → templates so your Host Groups reliably produce correct Kickstarts and disk layouts.

Kickstart templates are standard Anaconda files augmented with ERB so Satellite can inject host-specific variables at generation time. The typical pattern is to place static Kickstart directives and use ERB tags to substitute passwords, network settings, or activation keys. For example, setting the root password dynamically uses an ERB variable that Satellite replaces when creating the host-specific Kickstart.
